Part 1

Water on Earth: storage and phases

Where water is stored, and how it changes between solid, liquid and gas

Fun water fact: all of Earth's water in one sphere

Key idea

Gathered into one sphere, all of Earth's water is tiny next to the planet. Freshwater is tinier still.

Read the figure

  • The larger blue sphere holds all water on Earth: oceans, ice, groundwater, lakes, rivers and vapor
  • The smaller blue sphere next to it is freshwater

Connect it

In Lecture 4a you saw that freshwater is only about 2.5% of Earth's water, and most of that is locked in ice and groundwater.

Water storage on Earth

Key idea

Antarctica is the biggest body of freshwater storage, in the form of glaciers and ice.

Read the figure

Sphere size shows volume (km³) by continent for glaciers and ice caps (purple), groundwater (brown) and lakes, reservoirs and rivers (green).

Other stores

  • Water is also stored in the atmosphere, living organisms and soil
  • Humans store water artificially in reservoirs, tanks and rain barrels
  • Hydroelectric dams convert the water's potential energy into mechanical energy to generate electricity

Water changes phase as it moves between stores

Key idea

Water exists in three phases on the planet: solid, liquid and gas. In Banff you can see all three at once.

  • Solid: when water becomes very cold and freezes it becomes ice, which has a definite form and shape
  • Liquid: water takes the shape of its container in storage, or its channel as it moves
  • Gas: water in gas form is called water vapor

Read the photo

Glacier (solid) on the peaks, clouds (condensed vapor) above, lake (liquid) below.

Go further

Optional: a TED talk on a possible fourth phase of water.

The phase diagram of water

Key idea

When water changes phase, heat is absorbed or released without changing its temperature. This is latent (hidden) heat.

The diagram shows water's phase as a function of pressure and temperature.

  • 1 calorie: heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1 °C
  • Triple point (0.01 °C, 0.6 kPa): all three phases coexist in equilibrium
  • Melting point: temperature at which ice melts
  • Boiling point: temperature at which water evaporates (100 °C at 101 kPa)
  • Critical pressure: pressure needed to liquefy a gas at its critical temperature
  • Critical point (374 °C, 22,089 kPa): beyond it, water is a supercritical fluid, between gas and liquid

Phase changes and latent heat

Key idea

Moving toward gas absorbs heat from the environment; moving toward solid releases it.

Liquid ↔ gas (540–600 cal/g)

Evaporation absorbs the latent heat of vaporization; the most energetic molecules escape and the liquid cools. Condensation releases that heat.

Liquid ↔ solid (80 cal/g)

Melting requires heat. Freezing, the reverse, releases the latent heat of fusion.

Solid ↔ gas (about 680 cal/g)

Sublimation: solid directly to gas. Deposition: vapor directly to solid, such as frost.

Read the figure

Red arrows absorb heat from the environment; blue arrows release heat to it.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Where is most of Earth's freshwater stored, and in what form?

In Antarctica, as glaciers and ice.

Q2 What is latent heat? Give an example of a phase change that releases it.

Heat transferred to or from a substance that changes its phase but not its temperature. Condensation, freezing and deposition all release latent heat.

Q3 Which takes more energy per gram: melting ice or evaporating water? By roughly how much?

Evaporating water: about 540–600 cal/g versus 80 cal/g for melting, roughly 7 times more.

Part 2

Properties of water

Why the water molecule's shape makes water a solvent and gives it surface tension

The dipolar water molecule

Key idea

Water is a polar molecule: a slightly negative oxygen side and slightly positive hydrogen sides, which lets molecules hydrogen bond.

Within a molecule

Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom share electrons in covalent bonds, one of the strongest types of bonding within molecules. That is why water does not break down easily.

Between molecules

Because oxygen carries a slight negative charge, it attracts the hydrogen atoms of other water molecules. These hydrogen bonds (dashed lines in the figure) hold water molecules together.

Water as a universal solvent

Key idea

Because it is polar, water dissolves ionic and polar substances, which is vital for biology and for carrying dissolved material.

  • Many biochemical reactions happen only in aqueous solutions (cytoplasm, blood), and water transports biological molecules
  • Ionic and polar substances (acids, alcohols, salts) dissolve easily; nonpolar substances (fats, oils) do not
  • Nonpolar molecules stay together because it is more favorable for water molecules to hydrogen bond to each other

How dissolving works

An ion or polar compound in water is surrounded by small water molecules. Their negative ends face positive parts of the solute, and their positive ends face negative parts.

Cohesion, adhesion and surface tension

Key idea

Strong hydrogen bonds give water high cohesion and therefore surface tension.

  • Cohesion: water sticks to water. Small amounts on a non-soluble surface stay together as drops
  • Adhesion: water sticks to other materials
  • Surface tension: molecules at the surface have no neighbors above, so they pull harder on neighbors beside and below (center diagram)

Why it matters

Cohesion holds the water column together as it is pulled up through xylem in plants by transpiration. A liquid with lower surface tension would “rip,” forming air pockets that block the vessel.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q4 What kind of bond holds atoms together within a water molecule, and what kind holds separate water molecules together?

Within: covalent bonds. Between molecules: hydrogen bonds.

Q5 Why does salt dissolve in water but oil does not?

Salt is ionic, so polar water molecules surround and separate its ions. Oil is nonpolar, so water molecules bond to each other instead and the oil stays together.

Q6 How does surface tension help plants?

Cohesion keeps the water column in the xylem intact as transpiration pulls water upward, preventing air pockets.

Part 3

Energy and the global water cycle

How much water moves between ocean, air and land, and the energy that drives it

The global water cycle in numbers

Key idea

Over land, precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration; the surplus returns to the sea as river discharge.

Check the balance yourself

  • Land precipitation 111 − land evapotranspiration 65.5 = 45.5
  • That 45.5 equals the net vapor transport from ocean to land, and the river discharge back to the sea

Why climate matters

A warmer atmosphere holds much more water vapor than a cold one (think of seasonal humidity). The physics of vapor pressure versus temperature governs how the cycle will respond to global warming.

Surface energy balance

Key idea

Net radiation from the sun does three things: warms the surface, warms the air, and evaporates water.

dQ/dt = Rₙ − G − H − λE

  • Q: heat stored in the surface layer
  • Rₙ: net surface irradiance (net radiation)
  • G: ground heat flux
  • H: sensible heat flux (warms the air)
  • λE: latent heat flux (evaporation)

Read the figure

Of 342 W/m² incoming solar radiation, 168 is absorbed by the surface; 78 W/m² leaves as evapotranspiration (latent heat), far more than the 24 W/m² of thermals.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q7 Using the global water cycle figure, show that the land part of the cycle balances.

Land precipitation (111) − land ET (65.5) = 45.5, which equals both the net vapor transport to land and the river discharge to the sea (all in 10³ km³/yr).

Q8 In the surface energy balance, which term is the energy used to evaporate water?

λE, the latent heat flux.

Part 4

Water balance in a watershed

Conservation of mass: inflow − outflow = change in storage

Water balance and budget

Key idea

Inflow − Outflow = Change in storage, or I − O = ΔS.

Three universal rules of water on Earth

  • Water cannot be created or destroyed
  • Conservation of mass and energy applies
  • There is always a finite amount of water on Earth

Reading the sign of ΔS

  • Inflow > outflow → ΔS positive: storage increases over time
  • Inflow < outflow → ΔS negative: stored water is lost over time

Water balance in a watershed

Key idea

A detailed watershed balance tracks every way water enters and leaves, above and below ground.

P + GWᵢₙ = Qₒᵤₜ + GWₒᵤₜ + D + ET + ΔS

  • In: precipitation P, groundwater inflow GWᵢₙ
  • Out: streamflow Q, groundwater outflow GWₒᵤₜ (underflow), deep recharge D, evapotranspiration ET
  • ΔS: change in storage

Read the figure

The surface water divide and subsurface water divide need not match. This figure assumes GWᵢₙ = 0.

Conservation principle: what can we actually measure?

Key idea

A watershed is a control volume: it receives and releases water, and input − output = change in storage.

Simplify it

If Gᵢₙ and Gₒᵤₜ are negligible and long-term ΔS = 0, then P = ET + Q

ΔS = P + Gᵢₙ − (Q + ET + Gₒᵤₜ)

TermWhat it isHow we get it
PPrecipitationRain gauges
QRiver dischargeStream gauges
ETEvapotranspirationHard to get, except local values
GᵢₙGroundwater inHard to get; assume zero
GₒᵤₜGroundwater outHard to get; assume zero
SStorage (groundwater, rivers, lakes)Often hard to get

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q9 Over one year a watershed receives 1,200 mm of precipitation, loses 450 mm to ET and 700 mm to streamflow. Groundwater flows are negligible. What is ΔS?

ΔS = 1,200 − (450 + 700) = +50 mm: storage increased.

Q10 Which two terms of the watershed water balance are routinely measured, and with what?

P with rain gauges and Q with stream gauges.

Q11 Under what assumptions does the balance reduce to P = ET + Q?

Groundwater inflow and outflow are negligible, and over the long-term annual mean the change in storage is zero.

Part 5

Watersheds and streams

Delineating watersheds, stream order, and how streams differ in timing and groundwater connection

What is a watershed?

Key idea

A watershed is an area of land that drains to a common outlet: a lake, stream segment or bay.

The name depends on size

Basin > Catchment > Watershed > Sub-watershed

Streams in a watershed

A watershed usually contains streams of different width, volume and flow rate. Every stream is unique; slope and topography strongly control their direction and characteristics.

Read the figure

Snowpack and mountain ridges at the top, tributaries feeding a lake and main channel, the watershed boundary, a sub-basin, and the riparian zone along the river to the bay.

Delineating a watershed boundary by hand

Key idea

A watershed boundary always crosses topographic contours at a right angle.

1. Identify the watershed outlet

2. Identify nearby water courses and their direction of flow

3. Look for high points (ridges, mountain tops) and mark them

4. Visualize surface flow and mark arrows

5. Trace the outline starting from the outlet, connecting high points and crossing contours at right angles

Read the figure

Left: red circles mark high points, arrows show flow. Middle and right: a boundary drawn step by step on a contour map.

Stream order

Key idea

Stream order classifies a drainage network: two streams of the same order join to make the next order.

  • The smallest tributaries are first order
  • Two first-order streams join → second order
  • Two second-order streams join → third order

Orders range from 1st (smallest) to 12th (largest).

Size classes

  • Orders 1–3: headwater streams, in the upper watershed, often on steep slopes. Over 80% of the world's waterways
  • Orders 4–6: medium streams
  • Above 6 (up to 12): rivers

Notice in the figure that a 1st-order stream joining a 3rd-order stream does not change its order.

Types of streams: timing and water availability

Key idea

Streams differ in how often they flow, which depends on where the groundwater table sits relative to the streambed.

Perennial

Flows continuously. Continuous baseflow from a groundwater table that is generally above the streambed all year.

Intermittent

Flows part of the year. Baseflow at least once a year, usually in winter and spring when the water table rises above the streambed.

Ephemeral

Flows only in response to precipitation, during and shortly after (generally under 48 hours). Sits above the water table. Roadside ditches do not count.

All three stream types can exist in one watershed

Key idea

Walk uphill in a watershed and you often pass from perennial to intermittent to ephemeral channels.

Look at how the water in the channel changes: steady flow, scattered pools, then a dry, leaf-covered swale that carries water only after rain.

Types of streams: groundwater interactions

Key idea

Not all river water is surface runoff: groundwater seepage keeps rivers flowing between storms (baseflow).

Read the four panels

  • (a) Gaining: water table above the stream; groundwater flows into the channel
  • (b) Losing: water table below the stream; channel water seeps out to groundwater
  • (c) Disconnected: an unsaturated zone separates the stream from the water table
  • (d) Dry: the water table is far below the channel

The water still comes from precipitation, but not all of it arrives as surface runoff.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q12 What is the first step when delineating a watershed by hand, and how should the boundary cross contour lines?

First identify the outlet. The boundary crosses contours at right angles, connecting high points.

Q13 A 2nd-order stream joins a 1st-order stream. What is the order downstream? What if it joins another 2nd-order stream?

Joining a 1st-order stream: still 2nd order. Joining another 2nd-order stream: 3rd order.

Q14 Explain the difference between an ephemeral stream and a gaining stream in terms of the water table.

An ephemeral stream sits above the water table and flows only right after rain. A gaining stream has the water table above the streambed, so groundwater flows into it.
